title: How to help students understand what they don’t know
author: Ed Finkel
summary: Ed Finkel reports on how teachers can help students recognise the limits of their knowledge when they revisit topics from earlier grades and insist they have already learned them. Education researchers Jerry Rosiek, Michelle Jordan and Ying-Chih Chen agree that students confuse having some knowledge with real understanding. They recommend inquiry or Socratic dialogue and hands-on tasks that are deliberately designed to reveal where current knowledge falls short, starting from phenomena in students' daily lives. They also stress that teachers should treat uncertainty as productive rather than something to reduce to zero, and should help overconfident students without publicly shaming them. The calibration of difficulty matters: too simple bores students and too hard requires the teacher to scaffold.
points: Students often confuse having some knowledge with understanding, and the useful marker of knowledge is flexibility in applying it rather than recalling answers.
Tasks should be deliberately designed to reveal the limits of what students know, after which they are more open to hearing new content.
Starting with everyday phenomena, such as solar panels on nearby buildings, and probing why they work with Socratic questions exposes gaps students had not considered.
Teachers should avoid a gotcha tone, since students can feel whether the teacher is supportive of their changing their view or merely exposing them.
The level of uncertainty should be pitched so it is neither boring nor overwhelming, with the teacher stepping in as scaffold when it gets too hard.
quotes: You have to convince people that there are limits to their knowledge,” said Jerry Rosiek, education studies department head at University of Oregon's College of Education.

Generally, it’s assumed that the best way to do that is to get students involved in an inquiry or some sort of a dialogue, where their own knowledge of the topic is revealed to be inadequate,” said Rosiek.

The difference between someone who is good at trivia and someone who is truly knowledgeable is the adaptability and flexibility of their knowledge, said Jordan, whose research focuses on K-12 STEM education.

It has to be designed for the purpose of revealing the limits of their knowledge,” he said. “Then, the students are likely, you hope, to come out of that experience with the understanding that they don’t have the knowledge. Then they’re open to hearing more.

Nobody likes to be exposed publicly as having been wrong about something,” he said. “You can respond in a more fulsomely human way to the child in front of you. They can feel whether the teacher is playing ‘gotcha,’ or being supportive of the effort in changing their view of something.
Don’t leave them swimming in uncertainty,” Jordan said. “And don’t act as if the only valuable thing is reducing the uncertainty to zero. … Use it to elicit new wonderings.
